cur:catacombs-via-anapo-multiplication.summary: Against a light ground a young, beardless Christ in a long tunic and pallium bends forward and touches with a rod a row of seven baskets of bread at his feet. With a single figure and a row of baskets the painter evokes the feeding of the multitude, a sign of the Eucharist and of the heavenly banquet.
facts: The rod with which Christ touches the baskets is the usual sign of miraculous power in 4th-century Roman art.
The catacomb on the Via Anapo is anonymous: its ancient name is not known.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-144-chris.summary: The psalmist and his followers raise their hands in praise to the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos, who stands with a cross-staff in the centre of the heavens among angels with bannered wands and turns to bless them with an open hand. Below, an angel upholds a man who is falling, a family seated at a laden table gazes up at Christ — 'the eyes of all wait upon thee; and thou givest them their meat in due season' — and deer and cattle graze by streams.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
After centuries in England the manuscript arrived in Utrecht in 1716; it is often called the most valuable manuscript in the Netherlands.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-144-chris.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:manuscripts2-menologion-flight-into-.summary: The Virgin rides a donkey holding the Christ child, led by a young man and followed by Joseph, toward a towered city from whose gate a figure comes out to meet them. A hill rises behind them against the gold sky. The episode was commemorated in the Byzantine calendar in the days after Christmas.
facts: The Menologion of Basil II, made at Constantinople for Emperor Basil II (976–1025), holds about 430 miniatures by eight painters whose names — among them Pantoleon, Michael of Blachernai and Nestor — are written beside each image.
It covers only the first half of the church year, September to February, and passed through the hands of Ludovico Sforza, Duke of Milan, before Pope Paul V received it for the Vatican Library.
